ask/pretrained: Start from a pretrained language model, such as GPT. Trained on plain text to predict the next token, it does one thing: it continues the text it is given.
ask/prompt: That text is called the prompt: it prompts the model to go on, the way a cue prompts an actor. Give it the prompt capital of Peru?
ask/quiz: On the web, a question like that often sits in a list of quiz questions. So the model may simply carry on the list: capital of Chile?
ask/assistant: We want an assistant instead: a model that answers the person asking, here with Lima. Continuing web text is a different job from doing what someone asks.
ask/ouyang: In 2022, Long Ouyang and colleagues at OpenAI made that point, and hired labelers to write the reply they wanted for each of about thirteen thousand prompts.
ask/tune: Then they fine-tuned GPT-3, a much larger GPT, on those replies: they kept training it from its pretrained weights, just as with an image network.
ask/name: Each reply is a right answer that a person wrote down, like the label on a photo, and learning from given right answers is called supervised. So this is supervised fine-tuning: S F T.
sequence/write: To train on a conversation, write it out as one sequence of tokens: the question, then the reply. Nine tokens in all.
sequence/markers: Marker tokens say who is speaking. User, for the person asking, opens the question; assistant opens the reply; and end closes it. They come from a fixed template.
sequence/predict: Run the model over all nine, as in pretraining: it predicts each token from the ones before it.
sequence/bars: So every token after the first gets a loss, minus the log of the probability it was given, drawn here as a bar.
sequence/problem: The tallest bars are the question's: nobody can guess what will be asked. Grade them all, and much of the lesson teaches the model to write questions: exactly the habit to break.
mask/mask: So give each token a mask, m: a one if the assistant wrote it, and a zero if not.
mask/markers: The question gets zeros, and so do both markers: the template put them there, not the assistant.
mask/end: The end token gets a one. The assistant writes it when its reply is done, and predicting it is how the model learns to stop.
mask/off: Multiply each loss by its mask, and the question's bars switch off. Three are left: the reply's.
mask/context: The question stays in the input: the model reads it in order to answer, and is just not graded on it.
mask/lima: Lima was given a probability of zero point five, so its loss is minus ln zero point five: about zero point six nine.
mask/rest: The full stop's loss is zero point two two, and the end token's is zero point one one. The three add up to one point oh two.
mask/mean: The loss, L, is their average: divide by three, the number of ones in the mask, and not by all nine tokens. That gives about zero point three four.
mask/why: Dividing by the ones makes L the average cost of one reply token, however long the question was.
mask/formula: In symbols: L is the sum, over every position t, of m t times minus ln p t, divided by the sum of the mask.
longer/system: Some conversations open with a system prompt: instructions written before the first question, such as be brief. It is context too, so its tokens all get zeros.
longer/turns: A longer conversation takes turns: question, reply, question, reply. The assistant wrote every reply, so every reply gets ones, its own end token included.
longer/count: Here the replies have twenty tokens and ten. Twenty plus ten: thirty of the seventy-four tokens carry loss.
longer/lr: Then train as when fine-tuning any pretrained network: with a small learning rate, so the model keeps what pretraining taught it.
